sections.text: ## Mohandas Karamchand Gandhi (1869–1948)

metadata.title: Anti-Colonial Leaders: Gandhi, Nehru, Ho Chi Minh, Nkrumah, Nyerere

sections.text: ### What He Did

metadata.title: Anti-Colonial Leaders: Gandhi, Nehru, Ho Chi Minh, Nkrumah, Nyerere

sections.text: Gandhi's contribution is the development and demonstration of *Satyagraha* — "truth-force" or "soul-force" — as a systematic political strategy. This was not just passive resistance or nonviolence; it was a coherent doctrine about how to delegitimize power.

metadata.title: Anti-Colonial Leaders: Gandhi, Nehru, Ho Chi Minh, Nkrumah, Nyerere

sections.text: ### The Satyagraha Framework

metadata.title: Anti-Colonial Leaders: Gandhi, Nehru, Ho Chi Minh, Nkrumah, Nyerere

sections.text:
```
  SATYAGRAHA: THE LOGIC OF NONVIOLENT RESISTANCE
  ================================================

metadata.title: Anti-Colonial Leaders: Gandhi, Nehru, Ho Chi Minh, Nkrumah, Nyerere

sections.text:
Premise 1: Political authority rests on consent.
             (Even coercive authority requires compliance to function.)

metadata.title: Anti-Colonial Leaders: Gandhi, Nehru, Ho Chi Minh, Nkrumah, Nyerere

sections.text:
Premise 2: Colonialism requires the colonized to cooperate.
             (British India could not function without Indian
              civil servants, workers, soldiers, tax payments.)

metadata.title: Anti-Colonial Leaders: Gandhi, Nehru, Ho Chi Minh, Nkrumah, Nyerere

sections.text:
Premise 3: Withdraw consent → power withers.
             (Non-cooperation denies the colonizer the infrastructure
              it needs to maintain power.)

metadata.title: Anti-Colonial Leaders: Gandhi, Nehru, Ho Chi Minh, Nkrumah, Nyerere

sections.text:
Premise 4: Accept suffering without retaliation.
             (Violence from the colonized justifies colonial force.
              Nonviolent suffering delegitimizes it — especially
              when the metropolitan public can observe it.)

metadata.title: Anti-Colonial Leaders: Gandhi, Nehru, Ho Chi Minh, Nkrumah, Nyerere

sections.text:
The strategic context: Works when:
  ✓ Opponent has a public opinion to embarrass
  ✓ Opponent has rule-of-law commitments (even hypocritical ones)
  ✓ The violence of suppression is visible
  ✓ The nonviolent discipline can be maintained

metadata.title: Anti-Colonial Leaders: Gandhi, Nehru, Ho Chi Minh, Nkrumah, Nyerere

sections.text:
The strategic limits: Fails when:
  ✗ Opponent is indifferent to public opinion
    (Gandhi explicitly said his method would not work
     against Hitler or Stalin)
  ✗ The opponent uses total violence without media access
  ✗ Nonviolent discipline breaks down
```

sections.text: ### The Key Campaigns

metadata.title: Anti-Colonial Leaders: Gandhi, Nehru, Ho Chi Minh, Nkrumah, Nyerere

sections.text: **South Africa (1893–1914)**: Gandhi developed Satyagraha not in India but in South Africa, resisting discriminatory laws against the Indian community. The Phoenix Settlement near Durban (1904) and Tolstoy Farm (1910) were communal living experiments embedded in the organizing. He won partial concessions from Smuts.

metadata.title: Anti-Colonial Leaders: Gandhi, Nehru, Ho Chi Minh, Nkrumah, Nyerere

sections.text: **Non-Cooperation Movement (1920–22)**: First mass mobilization of Congress against British rule. Millions refused to pay taxes, attend British schools, buy British goods, serve in British courts. Call-off after Chauri Chaura (mob burned police station, killing 22) — Gandhi's insistence on nonviolent discipline over political momentum.

metadata.title: Anti-Colonial Leaders: Gandhi, Nehru, Ho Chi Minh, Nkrumah, Nyerere

sections.text: **Salt March (1930)**: 240-mile march to the sea at Dandi to make salt from seawater — defying the British salt tax. Brilliant choice: salt was universal (everyone needed it), the tax was universally resented, and making salt from the sea was visibly peaceful while being explicitly illegal. 60,000 arrested. World press coverage. The Salt March is the moment Gandhi's strategy reached global scale.

metadata.title: Anti-Colonial Leaders: Gandhi, Nehru, Ho Chi Minh, Nkrumah, Nyerere

sections.text: **Quit India Movement (1942)**: Launched during WWII; "Do or Die." British arrested the entire Congress leadership within days. Scattered revolts, railway sabotage, massive repression. Strategically mixed — disrupted the war effort, demonstrated the depth of resistance, but did not achieve immediate results.

metadata.title: Anti-Colonial Leaders: Gandhi, Nehru, Ho Chi Minh, Nkrumah, Nyerere

sections.text: **Independence (1947)**: The partition was Gandhi's greatest failure and deepest wound. He had argued for a unified Hindu-Muslim India; he got partition. The subsequent violence (communal riots, 1–2 million dead) horrified him. He was assassinated January 30, 1948, by a Hindu nationalist who blamed him for concessions to Muslims.

metadata.title: Anti-Colonial Leaders: Gandhi, Nehru, Ho Chi Minh, Nkrumah, Nyerere

sections.text: ### Gandhi's Contradictions

metadata.title: Anti-Colonial Leaders: Gandhi, Nehru, Ho Chi Minh, Nkrumah, Nyerere

sections.text:
Gandhi was complex in ways that matter:
- His early writings in South Africa were explicitly anti-Black African (he objected to Indians being classified with "kaffirs"); he later evolved
- His views on caste were inconsistent; he renamed untouchables "Harijans" (children of God) without substantively challenging the system
- His views on women's bodies were controlling and strange (celibacy as spiritual discipline imposed on others)
- He opposed industrialization and modern medicine in ways that conflicted with Indian development needs

metadata.title: Anti-Colonial Leaders: Gandhi, Nehru, Ho Chi Minh, Nkrumah, Nyerere

sections.text: These are real limitations. They don't erase the strategic contribution.

sections.text: Nehru is Gandhi's political partner and institutional successor — the figure who translated the independence movement into a functioning state. India's first Prime Minister (1947–64).

sections.text: KEY CHOICES (1947–64):

metadata.title: Anti-Colonial Leaders: Gandhi, Nehru, Ho Chi Minh, Nkrumah, Nyerere

sections.text:
1. PARLIAMENTARY DEMOCRACY
     Chose Westminster model over presidential
     Chose competitive elections from the start
     (Most new states chose one-party rule)

sections.text:
2. SECULAR STATE
     Constitutional secularism — state cannot favor any religion
     Despite founding in the context of Hindu nationalism

sections.text:
3. NON-ALIGNMENT
     Neither US nor Soviet bloc
     Founded Non-Aligned Movement with Tito, Nasser (1955 Bandung)

sections.text:
4. PLANNED ECONOMY
     Five-Year Plans (influenced by Soviet model)
     State-led industrialization: steel, dams, universities

     Mixed results — industrial base built; consumer economy starved

metadata.title: Anti-Colonial Leaders: Gandhi, Nehru, Ho Chi Minh, Nkrumah, Nyerere

sections.text:
5. FEDERALISM
     Organized states along linguistic lines (controversial)
     Protected minority rights constitutionally
     Maintained democratic elections across extraordinary diversity

sections.text: ### What Nehru Got Wrong

metadata.title: Anti-Colonial Leaders: Gandhi, Nehru, Ho Chi Minh, Nkrumah, Nyerere

sections.text: The Nehru-era failures are instructive:

metadata.title: Anti-Colonial Leaders: Gandhi, Nehru, Ho Chi Minh, Nkrumah, Nyerere

sections.text:
- **Bureaucratic socialism**: License Raj — 80+ government approvals to start a business — strangled economic growth until liberalization in 1991
- **Kashmir**: Nehru's handling of the accession left a permanent territorial dispute that remains unresolved
- **China**: Misjudged Chinese intentions; India-China War (1962) humiliating defeat
- **Succession**: Did not build institutions that could function without his personal authority; daughter (Indira Gandhi) inherited leadership, leading to dynastic democracy

metadata.title: Anti-Colonial Leaders: Gandhi, Nehru, Ho Chi Minh, Nkrumah, Nyerere

sections.text: **Ho's Operational Innovation**: He synthesized Maoist people's war doctrine with Vietnamese conditions. Key principle: guerrilla warfare is 20% military, 80% political. "The enemy will pass slowly from the offensive to the defensive. The blitzkrieg will transform itself into a war of long duration. Thus, the enemy will be caught in a dilemma: he has to drag out the war in order to win it and does not possess... the psychological and political means to fight a long drawn-out war."

metadata.title: Anti-Colonial Leaders: Gandhi, Nehru, Ho Chi Minh, Nkrumah, Nyerere

sections.text: ### Ho Chi Minh: The Complicated Figure

metadata.title: Anti-Colonial Leaders: Gandhi, Nehru, Ho Chi Minh, Nkrumah, Nyerere

sections.text:
Ho's movement achieved independence. It also:
- Implemented land reform campaigns that killed tens of thousands of "class enemies" (1953–56, estimates 5,000–170,000 killed)
- Built a one-party Communist state that imprisoned dissidents
- Conducted the war with tactics that included assassination of South Vietnamese officials and civilian terror

metadata.title: Anti-Colonial Leaders: Gandhi, Nehru, Ho Chi Minh, Nkrumah, Nyerere

sections.text: His opening the Vietnamese Declaration of Independence with the American Declaration's words was deliberately calculated — asking the US to honor its own stated principles. The US ignored it and supported the returning French anyway.

sections.text: ## Kwame Nkrumah (1909–1972)

metadata.title: Anti-Colonial Leaders: Gandhi, Nehru, Ho Chi Minh, Nkrumah, Nyerere

sections.text: ### What He Did

metadata.title: Anti-Colonial Leaders: Gandhi, Nehru, Ho Chi Minh, Nkrumah, Nyerere

sections.text: Nkrumah led the Gold Coast to independence in 1957 as Ghana — the first sub-Saharan African colony to gain independence from a European power. He then spent nine years attempting to build a socialist Pan-African state before a military coup removed him in 1966.

metadata.title: Anti-Colonial Leaders: Gandhi, Nehru, Ho Chi Minh, Nkrumah, Nyerere

sections.text:
```
  NKRUMAH'S GHANA: PROMISE AND FAILURE
  ======================================

metadata.title: Anti-Colonial Leaders: Gandhi, Nehru, Ho Chi Minh, Nkrumah, Nyerere

sections.text:
ACHIEVEMENTS (1957–1966):
  - First independence in sub-Saharan Africa
  - Volta Dam and Akosombo hydroelectric (infrastructure)
  - University of Ghana expanded; schools built
  - Pan-African ideology articulated (Organization of
    African Unity, 1963 — Nkrumah's initiative)

metadata.title: Anti-Colonial Leaders: Gandhi, Nehru, Ho Chi Minh, Nkrumah, Nyerere

sections.text:
FAILURES:
  - One-party state (1964): Ghana becomes one-party republic
  - Preventive Detention Act: political imprisonment without trial
  - Cult of personality: "Osagyefo" ("Redeemer")
  - Economic mismanagement: cocoa price collapse + debt
  - Expelled Western investors; failed to replace with
    competent state management
  - Military coup February 24, 1966 (while Nkrumah in Hanoi)

metadata.title: Anti-Colonial Leaders: Gandhi, Nehru, Ho Chi Minh, Nkrumah, Nyerere

sections.text:
THE PAN-AFRICAN VISION:
  Nkrumah argued that individual African states were
  too small to be economically viable or diplomatically
  powerful. Continental union = his goal.
  The Organization of African Unity (1963) was a pale
  shadow of his vision — member states defended
  sovereignty above all else.
  African Union (2002) = later partial realization.
```

metadata.title: Anti-Colonial Leaders: Gandhi, Nehru, Ho Chi Minh, Nkrumah, Nyerere

sections.text: ### Nkrumah's Intellectual Legacy

metadata.title: Anti-Colonial Leaders: Gandhi, Nehru, Ho Chi Minh, Nkrumah, Nyerere

sections.text: Despite his political failure, Nkrumah's ideological contribution was substantial. *Consciencism* (1964) attempted to synthesize African communalism, Islam, and Western philosophy. *Neo-Colonialism* (1965) argued that formal independence without economic independence was meaningless — that Western capital controlled African economies as effectively as colonial administration had. This framework (often called "dependency theory" in academic form) became the standard left-nationalist analysis of post-colonial economies.

sections.text: ## Julius Nyerere (1922–1999)

metadata.title: Anti-Colonial Leaders: Gandhi, Nehru, Ho Chi Minh, Nkrumah, Nyerere

sections.text: ### What He Did

metadata.title: Anti-Colonial Leaders: Gandhi, Nehru, Ho Chi Minh, Nkrumah, Nyerere

sections.text: Nyerere led Tanganyika to independence in 1961, then united it with Zanzibar to form Tanzania in 1964. He served as President until 1985 — then voluntarily retired, one of the few African heads of state to step down voluntarily.

metadata.title: Anti-Colonial Leaders: Gandhi, Nehru, Ho Chi Minh, Nkrumah, Nyerere

sections.text: **Ujamaa (African socialism):**

metadata.title: Anti-Colonial Leaders: Gandhi, Nehru, Ho Chi Minh, Nkrumah, Nyerere

sections.text:
```
  NYERERE'S UJAMAA EXPERIMENT
  =============================

metadata.title: Anti-Colonial Leaders: Gandhi, Nehru, Ho Chi Minh, Nkrumah, Nyerere

sections.text:
Theory: African traditional communalism → socialist development
          Bypassing capitalist stage → directly to socialism
          "African socialism": extended family as economic unit

metadata.title: Anti-Colonial Leaders: Gandhi, Nehru, Ho Chi Minh, Nkrumah, Nyerere

sections.text:
Implementation: Villagization
  - Arusha Declaration (1967): nationalization of major industries
  - Ujamaa villages: forced resettlement of rural population
    into collectivized villages (1973-76)
  - 11 million people moved; agricultural production collapsed
  - Tanzania's economy declined throughout 1970s

metadata.title: Anti-Colonial Leaders: Gandhi, Nehru, Ho Chi Minh, Nkrumah, Nyerere

sections.text:
What worked:
  - Education: adult literacy from 10% to 90%
  - Health: basic medical infrastructure
  - Political stability: no coups; peaceful transitions
  - Swahili as national language: national unity

metadata.title: Anti-Colonial Leaders: Gandhi, Nehru, Ho Chi Minh, Nkrumah, Nyerere

sections.text:
What failed:
  - Agricultural collectivization: complete economic failure
  - Industrial nationalization: inefficiency and collapse
  - By 1985: GDP lower than at independence in some metrics

metadata.title: Anti-Colonial Leaders: Gandhi, Nehru, Ho Chi Minh, Nkrumah, Nyerere

sections.text:
Nyerere's response:
  "We chose the wrong policies but for the right reasons.
  We were not a corrupt government."
  He acknowledged the villagization failure explicitly.
```

metadata.title: Anti-Colonial Leaders: Gandhi, Nehru, Ho Chi Minh, Nkrumah, Nyerere

sections.text:
**The Tanzania-Uganda War (1979)**: Nyerere ordered Tanzanian forces to invade Uganda, which toppled Idi Amin. This was:
- Illegal under OAU norms (non-interference in member states)
- Morally defensible (Amin had killed 300,000+ Ugandans)
- Practically successful (Amin fell)
- A template later cited for "humanitarian intervention" doctrine

metadata.title: Anti-Colonial Leaders: Gandhi, Nehru, Ho Chi Minh, Nkrumah, Nyerere

sections.text: **Voluntary Retirement (1985)**: Nyerere stepped down before his party forced him out. His economic policies had failed; he chose to leave rather than cling to power. This remains remarkable in African political history.

sections.text: ## Comparison Table

metadata.title: Anti-Colonial Leaders: Gandhi, Nehru, Ho Chi Minh, Nkrumah, Nyerere

sections.text:
| Figure | Country | Period | Method | Institutional Outcome |
|--------|---------|--------|--------|----------------------|
| Gandhi | India | 1919–1947 | Satyagraha; mass civil disobedience | Indian independence; personally killed; Pakistan partition |
| Nehru | India | 1947–1964 | Parliamentary democracy; planned economy | Stable democracy; economic mixed results |
| Ho Chi Minh | Vietnam | 1945–1969 | People's war; united front nationalism | Vietnam unified 1975; one-party communist state |
| Nkrumah | Ghana | 1957–1966 | Pan-African socialism | Deposed; legacy: Pan-African ideology; Ghana democratized later |
| Nyerere | Tanzania | 1961–1985 | Ujamaa; African socialism | Stable; literacy/health gains; economic failure; voluntary retirement |
